peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We would like to thank the reviewers for their thoughtful and helpful critiques of our work. The work is greatly improved upon the incorporation of their suggestions.
Reviewer #1:
Wei et al describe the first single cell sequencing atlas for S. japonicum—the human-infective Asian blood fluke. This is a really impressive study; with approx. 100k cells it’s the largest single cell atlas produced in schistosome research—creating a rich new resource for understanding schistosome development. The high cell coverage and inclusion of intermediate stages of development has enabled the authors to produce high resolution data on the sexual-tissue development, uncover distinct neural lineages and reveal novel biological insights into sexual signalling/development in schistosomes.
A key highlight of the work is the discovery of a male-specific neural circuit that directly mediates female development. The discovery builds upon previous research in S. mansoni demonstrating that nrps in males produces the pheromone BATT, which is essential for male-stimulated female development. The authors report a neural cell type (“delta-3”) that expresses nrps, and the S. japonicum homologue of lsamp, which expresses a neural surface protein in other species. The authors functionally characterise lsamp, confirming its expression in delta-3 cells and showing that it is required for BATT production but affects neither delta-3 development nor nrps expression. They further show that lsamp expression is closely colocated with the axons and synaptic junctions of a ventral neural network. Knocking down lsamp disrupts this network. The authors suggest that lsamp is required for males to produce or maintain neural fibrils.
Overall, this is exciting work that deepens our understanding of sexual signalling and development in these obligate dioecious parasites. The work is highly significant within the parasitology field and will be of broader interest for developmental biologists.
It is a large body of work and, in places, the manuscript is currently hard to navigate. There are some sections that may benefit from simplifying/streamlining, including some analyses that didn’t seem strictly necessary. We also felt that there were aspects of the functional characterisation, where the authors have over-reached in their interpretations.
We sincerely appreciate your recognition of the novelty of our work. In line with your constructive suggestions, we have carefully revised the manuscript to enhance readability by simplifying analyses that were not central to the core narrative and by cautiously refining the interpretations of certain functional characterizations. Our detailed responses are provided below.
Specific comments - Major points
1. To validate clusters (S. Fig 3), some of the hybridization patterns are unclear. Presenting evidence for the more diffuse tissues is difficult. Nevertheless, ctsb, tpm2, syn2 do look very similar.
Thank you for your feedback. We fully agree that the extensive distribution of tissues like muscle and tegument makes it challenging to resolve specific cell identities based solely on WISH patterns. To definitively discriminate between such broadly expressed but distinct cell types, we performed double-FISH in male worms, using published marker genes (such as tal for tegument and tpm2 for muscle) and the novel marker genes (slc7a14 for syncytial, slc6a5 for parenchymal, and cpb for muscle) identified in our study.
As shown in the revised Supplementary Fig. 4, the results confirmed that the previously reported tegument marker tal and the muscle marker tpm2, though both widely expressed, labeled distinct cell types (Supplementary Fig. 4a). Similarly, the newly identified parenchymal marker slc6a5 (Supplementary Fig. 4b) and syncytial marker slc7a14 (Supplementary Fig. 4c) did not colocalize with tpm2—a pattern particularly evident in the oral sucker of male worms (Supplementary Fig. 4c, lower panels). Furthermore, the novel muscle-associated marker gene cpb showed complete colocalization with tpm2, confirming its expression in muscle cells (Supplementary Fig. 4d). Together, these findings resolve cellular identities that were ambiguous from WISH data alone and further validate the clustering accuracy of our single-cell RNA sequencing data. These results have now been incorporated into the revised manuscript (908–915).
2. Describing the proportions of cell types is quite prominent in the manuscript (incl. Figs 1 c and d), but how informative is this analysis, beyond an extremely crude look? Sorting, library prep etc. creates bias for certain cell-types (e.g. more round cells like stem cells are favoured by sorting) and can distort recovered cell numbers. In previously published works, actual cell abundance vs cell captured by the scRNAseq process differ wildly, affecting differing cell types unequally. Some of the numbers make sense, like the expansion of vitellaria in females, but others make less sense like the much higher abundance of flame cells than gut cells. There’s a vague/superficial statement, which could be removed to save space, about there being ~20% neural and neoblast cell types when the numbers actually differ quite markedly between timepoints. Abundance across the whole dataset is shown in S Fig 5; yes it does broadly confirm some expectations but it doesn’t really shed any new light. And some of the findings seem counter-intuitive: like the proportion of muscle cells from males.
Thank you for raising this important point. We agree that inferring absolute cell type proportions from scRNA-seq data can be misleading due to technical biases introduced during cell dissociation, sorting, and library preparation. Although all samples were processed under the same protocol, making relative comparisons feasible, we fully acknowledge that these biases may result in the over- or under-representation of certain cell types. In line with your suggestion, we have now swapped the positions of the previous Supplementary Fig. 5 (showing abundance across the whole dataset) and Fig. 1c-d, removed statements regarding approximate proportions of neural and neoblast cells, and revised the manuscript to tone down and better contextualize descriptions of cell type abundances throughout in lines 149-159.
3. The authors performed subcluster analysis on sexual tissues and neoblast populations, from which they define 17 sub-types. The rationale for their naming scheme is not clear and abbreviations need to be explained. A discontinuous series from the Greek alphabet, plus some numbering (i.e. alpha, beta, gamma-1, gamma-2, delta, epsilon, kappa, nu) is used. Previously, a similar scheme has been used in published descriptions of S. mansoni stem cells (see doi.org/10.1016/j.pt.2021.03.005). It’s not clear if published delta, epsilon, and kappa sub-types are equivalent to those reported here. Distinguishing between 17 populations in the figures (S Fig 6a and Fig 2) is also challenging. Perhaps a numerical key could be added to help readability?
Apologies for the confusion. To improve clarity in the naming scheme of neoblast subpopulations, we have replaced the Greek-letter designations with a numerical system in the revised Fig. 2b, Supplementary Fig. 7 and 9. The updated names are: SSCs-1 (formerly alpha), SSCs-2 (formerly beta), SSCs-5 (formerly gamma-1), SSCs-6 (formerly gamma-2), SSCs-7 (formerly delta), SSCs-3 (formerly epsilon), SSCs-4 (formerly kappa).
As you noted, a previous study on stem cells in S. mansoni asexual (sporocyst) and sexual (juvenile) stages designated certain populations as delta, epsilon, and kappa subtypes (PMID: 29988015). To aid comparison, we examined the expression of orthologous stem cell marker genes in our dataset, which provides a cross-reference between the stem cell populations of S. mansoni and S. japonicum. As shown in the revised dot plots (Supplementary Fig. 7b–c), SSCs-1 to SSCs-4 exhibit strong similarity to δ-cells, characterized by high expression of fgfra, fgfrb, hes2, and tp53. SSCs-5 and SSCs-6 likely correspond to ε-cells, marked by elevated expression of astf and bhlh (PMID: 33893056). Furthermore, to enhance figure readability, we have regenerated the UMAP plots with a clear numerical key (Fig. 2b, and Supplementary Fig. 7a).
4. RNA velocity analysis was performed on the sex related subsets, revealing trajectories (Fig 2b) that made sense like the GSC -> GSC progeny in both sexes and the S1 vitellocytes ->->late vitellocyte. There are also a lot of arrows converging on the centre (SSC beta?) that aren’t mentioned. Further subsetting (Fig 2c) reveals trajectories from GSC to gametes in males but the equivalent analysis is not at all convincing in females (contrary to the main text). In Fig 2c the four panels show a lot of redundant information and could be reduced to two panels.
Thank you for these valuable suggestions. We agree with the reviewer that the RNA velocity analysis shows arrows converging on the center, likely around SSCs-2 (formerly beta). In the original version, we focused on the vitellaria lineage in females, but these central arrows may indeed represent putative progenitor differentiation events that occur in both sexes. We have added a discussion of this point to the Discussion section in lines 484-490: “Although our RNA velocity analysis of sex-related subsets revealed clear trajectories from GSCs to their progeny, it consistently showed convergence toward a central cell state identified as SSCs-2 in both sexes (Fig. 2b). We hypothesize that this convergence point represents a shared, multipotent progenitor pool that functions as a developmental hub, capable of giving rise to multiple downstream cell types in both males and females. This finding offers new insight into the hierarchical organization of gonadal cells in this organism, suggesting the presence of a common—rather than sex-specific—early developmental regulatory mechanism.”
For the observed differences in germline cell trajectories between males and females, we carefully re-examined the RNA velocity analyses. Although the female GSC dataset is of reasonably high quality (as shown in the Response Fig. 1a), phase plots of high-confidence genes revealed that female cells lacked sufficient splicing signal (e.g., Sjc-0008397, Sjc-0003894, Sjc-0006007), whereas male cells displayed the expected almond-shaped distributions (as shown in the Response Fig. 1b). This deficiency in splicing information likely accounts for the noisy and inconsistent velocity directions observed in females. Additional factors may include sparse sampling of intermediate states or potential sex-specific splicing dynamics. Given these limitations, we concluded that RNA velocity is less suitable for inferring female GSC trajectories. Accordingly, the RNA velocity plots have been removed from the figures and manuscript text accordingly. Trajectory inference was subsequently performed employing the more robust expression-based method (lines 678-687, Slingshot (PMID: 30089906), as detailed in the revised Fig. 2c-d and lines 195-198.
In the revised Fig. 2c-d, we have retained two panels for each to improve clarity for readers: the left panel displays the cellular subclusters, while the right panel shows the pseudotime trajectories.
Response Figure1. Evaluation of sequencing data quality and RNA velocity fit on male and female GSCs. (a) Quality control summary of male and female GSCs. Left: UMI counts per cell in male and female datasets, with a nUMI cutoff of 1,500 indicated by the line. Middle: Number of genes detected per cell, with a nGene cutoff of 1,000 indicated by the line. Right: Transcript complexity in male and female datasets, with a log GenesPerUMI cutoff of 0.8 indicated by the line. (b) Phase portraits of the top 5 genes with the highest likelihood in female (top) and male (bottom) GSCs, as calculated by scVelo.
5. There’s quite a long section on clustering male and female specific genes. The authors reveal a cluster of genes with opposite temporal patterns between the sexes. It’s also interesting to note that for the majority of sex-specific genes, the temporal pattern is different between the sexes, with male genes reducing and female genes increasing. However, some of the methods and figures in this long section are difficult to navigate and it’s disappointing that the section is left quite open-ended with no further analysis of the 47 C1 genes. The overall conclusion is that the process is complex and involves modules of genes. Without the composition of the modules being described, it doesn’t really provide anything new.
The main text (L201+) and legend for Fig 7 really need signposts to the relevant section of Methods because it’s not immediately obvious that trajectories are the input for the sex-specific analyses. Even after the gam R description is found, it’s still unclear exactly what the inputs are and how the lists of 693, 750 and 156 relate — are they mutually exclusive? If not, overlaps should be indicated. In Fig 7b, pseudotime=0 is presented in the centre, so that one panel reads right-to-left and the other reads left-to-right; that seems counter-intuitive. How were the datasets clustered? It looks like the cluster number was set to 5 in each case, but it’s not clear why, when several clusters could have been further divided and some possibly merged. What is the dotted line on each cladogram?
Thank you for these detailed and constructive comments. To address your concerns, we have completely re-analyzed this section and revised both the Methods and Figures to improve clarity and informativeness.
In the revised manuscript, we applied the tradeSeq R package (PMID: 32139671) (Methods, lines 688–699) to identify temporally dynamic genes along male and female germline pseudotime trajectories separately. Using a stringent p-value cutoff (1e-10), we robustly defined dynamic gene sets for each sex (revised Supplementary Fig. 8, and Data 8-9). This new analysis replaces the previous version that included the 47 C1 genes and the three gene lists (693, 750, and 156), resolving the previous ambiguities and improving interpretability.
To enhance biological interpretation, we have supplemented the description of module composition with detailed functional enrichment analyses of the genes in each module (lines 193-222). We firstly performed GO enrichment analysis on the dynamic gene modules to reveal the biological processes associated with each cluster (revised Supplementary Fig. 8, and Data 10-11). A full list of module genes is provided in Supplementary Data 8-9, 12 to ensure transparency. The number of clusters was determined using the getClusters function in ClusterGVis, which applies the Elbow method to evaluate within-cluster sum of squares (Methods, lines 694-699). We further incorporated a focused analysis of known germline regulators (e.g., oc-1, nanos-1, eled, boule, nuob, meiob, and horm-2), along with newly identified candidates—ribc2 and Sjc-0003040—which are highly expressed in the late germline cells of males and females, respectively (revised Fig. 2e-g). Their pseudotime expression profiles are now shown explicitly, providing finer resolution into the regulatory programs underlying schistosome GSC differentiation (revised Fig. 2c-d). Taken together, we have revised this section to be more concise and included clearer conclusions (lines 193-218).
To improve clarity, explicit cross-references have been added in the main text (line 239) and in the legend of Supplementary Fig. 8, directing readers to the relevant Methods section describing the trajectory-based identification of dynamic genes (lines 688-699). The revised Supplementary Fig. 8 focuses on pseudotime trajectories and gene dynamics patterns for each sex separately, with reorganized orientation and removal of the dashed lines automatically generated by the ComplexHeatmap R package. In addition, we identified shared dynamic genes between male and female datasets by taking the intersection of their respective dynamic gene sets, and we now provide a comprehensive list of genes dynamically expressed in both sexes across each cluster as updated Supplementary Data 12.
6. After the module analysis, the narrative returned to trajectory analysis using RNA velocity. The authors were unable to connect stem cell development to vitellaria development but were able to show trajectory from S1 vitellocyte to S1 progeny, with the latter marked by esg-2a expression. The paragraph finishes with a rather bland statement that the work aligned with previous findings and provides new insights. Vf1 expression was known, but the esg-2a expression later in differentiation is new. What else switched on later? Having established a convincing trajectory, was it not possible to mine further information on genes expressed early vs late? Likewise, the analysis of Mehlis’ gland is interesting but only two strong markers are shown in Supplementary Figure 6. Could no other markers be found?
Thank you for these suggestions. We performed sub-clustering and trajectory analysis of vitelline cells to provide a finer resolution of their differentiation from S1 to late vitelline cells (revised Supplementary Fig. 9). Sub-clustering identified eight distinct subtypes, including S1, S1 progeny, early vitellocytes (EVi), and late vitellocytes (LVi) (Supplementary Fig. 9a, and Data 13). Slingshot trajectory inference revealed two potential differentiation branches (Lineage 1 and Lineage 2; Supplementary Fig. 9c–d). Evaluation of differentiation potential using CytoTRACE (PMID: 31974247) indicated that only Lineage 1 exhibits high differentiation potential (Supplementary Fig. 9e). Using the tradeSeq R package (PMID: 32139671) to analyze the gene expression dynamics along these lineages, we found, in addition to the known marker vf1, genes such as p48 and the newly identified esg-2a display a gradual increase in expression along Lineage 1 (Supplementary Fig. 9f). These findings support the designation of Lineage 1 as the primary vitelline developmental pathway. Furthermore, to address your comment, we have provided a set of significantly dynamic genes identified along the vitelline pseudotime (Supplementary Data 14), encompassing genes exhibiting high expression at distinct stages of vitelline cell differentiation, including both early- and late-stage–enriched genes.
The functional composition of each gene module involved in Lineage 1 differentiation was summarized by GO term enrichment (Supplementary Data 15), and a complete marker gene list is provided (Supplementary Data 13) to enable readers to explore candidate regulators in detail.
For the Mehlis’ gland, we extended the analysis beyond the two strong markers originally shown in Supplementary Fig. 6c (now named Supplementary Fig. 11c). Additional candidate marker genes have now been identified and are included in the revised Supplementary Data 7, providing a more comprehensive molecular characterization of this organ.
The above content has been updated in the manuscript lines 223-253.
7. The authors subset the neuronal data and recluster into a highly connected UMAP showing at least 5 lineages. This is an important part of the reference resource created by the project. However, the authors should maybe avoid using nomenclature based on Greek letters, given that it is already used for stem cells, including within the same paper. How about just numbering them? Over time, more functional names will be applied but, for now, it might suffice to name them as neural lineage 1, etc. Or maybe use N1, etc? The more granular names like delta-3 would then become N4.3.
Thank you for the suggestion. We have simplified the nomenclature of neuronal populations by adopting a consistent numerical system (e.g., N1–N5). Specifically, Pre. alpha has been renamed N1. p, with its derivatives designated as N1.1 Neuron (alpha-1 Neuron) and N1.2 Neuron (alpha-2 Neuron). Similarly, Pre. beta is now N2. p, giving rise to N2.1 Neuron (beta-1 Neuron) and N2.2 Neuron (beta-2 Neuron). Pre. gamma has been renamed N3. p, with its sub-lineages renamed N3.1 Neuron (gamma-1 Neuron) and N3.2 Neuron (gamma-2 Neuron). For the delta lineage, Pre. delta and related progenitors are now designated as N4. p1–N4. p3, while the corresponding neuronal subtypes are renamed N4.1–N4.4 Neurons (delta-1 to delta-4 Neurons). In addition, epsilon Neuron has been renamed N5 Neuron. All figures (Fig. 3, and Supplementary Fig. 12-19) have been updated to reflect this revised nomenclature.
8. The authors use Slingshot to define lineages and derive pseudotime from their neural UMAP. How well does the pseudotime derived from these Slingshot trajectories agree with the sample-time metadata? (does a UMAP coloured by sample show differential enrichment for earlier or later parts of the trajectories?). The subsequent RNA velocity analysis agrees well with their pseudotime predictions, and Cell Rank is used to define terminal states (fully differentiated cells?). Similar to the earlier section on gamete development, the signposting to the methods is not very clear in the text - it’s not immediately clear the purpose of each analysis until reading further into the paper. Cell Rank is not mentioned in the legend to S Fig 10 and “dpt pseudotime” is not explained. The PAGA analysis, resulting in a network of pie charts (Fig. S10e and 11e), isn’t clear. What exactly is this showing? Is it really needed?
Thank you for your insightful comments on the neural lineage analysis. To examine how pseudotime inferred from Slingshot trajectories corresponds to actual sample collection times, we visualized the pseudotime distributions across samples using density plots, which were performed separately for male and female samples. The results show a clear alignment, with earlier samples enriched at the beginning of the trajectories and later samples at the terminal ends. The new plots illustrating this concordance have been added (Supplementary Fig. 12-13c).
As noted by the reviewer, the terminal states defined by CellRank can indeed be regarded as fully differentiated cells. This interpretation is consistent with the original CellRank publications (PMID: 35027767), where terminal states were shown to correspond to mature cell types in systems such as pancreatic lineage development and human hematopoiesis.
To improve clarity for readers, we added further details in the Methods section (lines 709–713) and explicitly mentioned the use of CellRank in Supplementary Fig. 12-13. We also clarified that “dpt pseudotime” refers to Diffusion Pseudotime (DPT) as calculated using scVelo (PMID: 32747759, lines 266-268 and 706-708).
Finally, to simplify the presentation and avoid potential confusion, we have removed the PAGA analysis and associated pie-chart network figures, as suggested.
9. Reviewer #3:
In this manuscript, You et al. identified a key gene required for male schistosome-triggered female reproductive maturation in Schistosoma japonicum. Specifically, they applied single-cell transcriptomics, RNA velocity and pseudotime analysis, and RNA in situ hybridization to reveal the cellular and molecular dynamics underlying this process. By focusing on four key time points, they uncovered putative developmental trajectories of male and female cells, focusing on germ cells and various neuronal cell types. Notably, the authors found that one of the three male-specific neuron subtypes, delta-3 neurons, relies on lsamp for normal axonal growth and ventral nerve network formation in the gynecophoric canal of male parasites. Through RNA interference experiments, they demonstrated that defects in this male nerve network due to lsamp knockdown reduce pheromone BATT production and subsequently impair female sexual development. Overall, this study provided a comprehensive single-cell transcriptomic dataset of both male and female S. japonicum during the important male-female pairing process and discovered a male nerve network critical for female reproductive development. The paper is well-written with high-quality figures that present solid experimental evidence. Beyond the important discovery of the role of lsamp in BATT signaling and its contribution to understanding this new signaling molecule, this work provides a useful resource for understanding schistosome development and reproductive biology. Thus, it is well suited for publication here. However, there are a few places where results are over-interpreted or alternative interpretations are not considered. Some suggestions for issues the authors should consider addressing in a revised manuscript are listed below.
We sincerely thank the reviewer for the thorough review and for recognizing the value of our single-cell transcriptomic dataset and the biological insights into male–female reproductive interactions in Schistosoma japonicum. In the revised manuscript, we have carefully addressed your concerns. Our detailed responses are provided below.
1. Some of the language used to describe cell states identified via single-cell sequencing overinterprets what has actually been learned. For example, male gametes are sperm and female gametes are oocytes. Since transcripts defining the “gamete” clusters are not presented in high-magnification FISH images, it is not clear whether these clusters reflect mature gametes or earlier stages along the differentiation pathway. Similarly, the cluster referred to as neural stem cells has not been validated in a way that allows them to be called stem cells. No evidence is presented that they self-renew, one of the defining features of stem cells. This could be a large pool of neural progenitors. In the absence of evidence that these cells are actual gametes or neural stem cells, the authors should soften their language.
Thank you. We agree that the terminology should be more precise. Accordingly, we have softened the language throughout the manuscript by replacing “male/female gametes” with more accurate descriptors such as “late male/female germ cells,” consistent with the previously published single-cell atlas of S. mansoni (PMID: 32973030). In addition, we have relabeled “neural stem cells” as “neural progenitor cells”.
2. The authors conclude that “LSAMP is essential for nerve fiber growth by stabilizing microtubules” (line 410). Since lsamp does not appear to be expressed in the affected neurons, it is unclear how it would act to stabilize their microtubules. Based on what is known about LSAMP function, it seems much more likely that the affected neurons are not able to extend their axons to the appropriate targets (or maintain them there), so any impact on microtubules would be secondary (i.e., there are no axonal microtubules because there may be no axons, not because the microtubules are less stable).
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful and critical assessment of our proposed mechanism. We fully agree that LSAMP's established function as a cell-surface adhesion molecule makes an extracellular mechanism—namely, axon guidance and target recognition—far more plausible than a direct, intracellular role in microtubule stabilization. Accordingly, we now interpret the observed reduction in axonal microtubules as a secondary morphological consequence reflecting the failure of nerve fiber maintenance and retraction, not a primary molecular impairment. To address this, we have removed the original statement and revised the text in lines 407–410: “These data suggest that LSAMP is essential for nerve fiber maintenance, likely by mediating appropriate axon guidance and target recognition. The observed alterations in microtubules may represent a secondary morphological consequence of impaired axon maintenance.”
3. Understanding the phenotype of lsamp RNAi parasites requires the authors to provide much more detail about the RNAi protocol and the subsequent phenotypic analysis. As written, it is unclear when the male parasites treated with dsRNA were initially harvested from the host. If they were harvested at 4 weeks or later, then lsamp is required to maintain the structure of the neural network (because it would have developed already). If they were harvested earlier, it is important to know when, so the reader can place the phenotype in the context of the developmental time course shown in Fig. 5e. The authors should also clarify the time points used for the subsequent analysis of the lsamp RNAi phenotypes. Were all assays conducted at 21 days post-pairing, or were some phenotypes examined at other time points? The graph in Supp. Fig. 22 overinterprets what is known. It is not clear that LSAMP guides the ventral neural network. Their RNAi experiment shows a single undefined endpoint from an undefined starting point.
We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising these important points regarding the experimental timeline and interpretation. We have added the detailed information about the RNAi protocol in the Methods (lines 721-730).
Indeed, the adult male parasites (26 dpi) used in the RNAi assay have already established their ventral neural network. Therefore, our results more likely support the conclusion that LSAMP is required for maintaining the neural network rather than for its initial development, as you suggested. To avoid potential misunderstanding, we have removed the previous Supplementary Fig. 23 and revised the related sections of the manuscript accordingly.
4. The conclusion that the affected axons transport BATT precursors is not supported by the data; other interpretations are possible. The authors begin their argument with the claim that “synaptic vesicles also transport other small molecules, such as the precursors for BATT (β-alanine and tryptamine)38, 39.” As far as I could tell, neither of these references mentions β-alanine or tryptamine. It remains an open question whether these compounds are transported via synaptic vesicles, released via solute carrier proteins, or if some other mechanism is at work. Furthermore, although the authors note that ddc (aadc) is required for ovary formation in planarians, they do not mention that it is also required for BATT production and is co-expressed with nrps in planarians, where it is likely producing tryptamine from tryptophan in the BATT-producing cells (PMID: 38889152). The lack of a phenotype in the ddc RNAi parasites could easily be due to insufficient knockdown (Supp. Fig. 18). Because ddc (aadc) is co-expressed with nrps in schistosomes, it seems most likely that the tryptamine is produced locally, rather than transported. If not, why is ddc (aadc) expressed in these cells?
We thank the reviewer for their insightful comments, which have significantly strengthened our manuscript. We have removed unsupported statements about β-alanine/tryptamine transport via synaptic vesicles. β-alanine is a known substrate for vesicular uptake systems, specifically via the vesicular GABA transporter (VGAT), for subsequent exocytotic release， and relevant citations (PMIDs: 7746489, 8897468, 38103629) have been added in lines 398-402.
We agree with your interpretation regarding local tryptamine synthesis, given the conserved co-expression of ddc and nrps in schistosomes, as previously reported in planarians (PMID: 38889152). Accordingly, the weak ddc RNAi phenotype observed in our study is likely attributable to insufficient knockdown, since DDC provides the essential substrate for BATT synthesis (updated Supplementary Fig. 21). We have therefore cited this study (PMID: 38889152) and incorporated a discussion of this point into the revised manuscript in lines 516-521: “The lack of an observable phenotype, despite significant knockdown, could be due to residual enzymatic activity being sufficient to maintain function, or possibly compensation through alternative pathways. We also acknowledge that the incomplete knockdown may have contributed to the absence of a pronounced phenotype. Future studies employing more potent interference strategies or conditional knockout approaches will be necessary to conclusively determine ddc's functional role”.
Consequently, we have reframed our model: While axonal transport is essential, tryptamine is more likely synthesized locally within nrps⁺ cells, whereas β-alanine—the other precursor of BATT—may be delivered via axonal cargo. Corresponding figures (Fig. 5f, and Supplementary Fig. 28) have been updated.

9. Figure 1C, S5, and Data S5 showed changes in cell type compositions across different time points. These measurements are relative, meaning a significant expansion of one cell type may cause a noticeable reduction of other cell types in proportion. Please provide a plot or table with absolute cell counts.
Following your suggestion, we have added a table (updated Supplementary Data 6) reporting the absolute cell counts for each cell type across all samples corresponding to the updated Fig. 1c, Supplementary Fig. 6a, and Data 5.
10. Line 170: eled is referred to as a germline cell marker, but it is also expressed in vitellaria and neoblasts in the posterior growth zone in juveniles. Can the authors comment on the eled+ cells in males that appear to be in vitellocytes at 22dpi (Fig. 1d)?
We appreciate the reviewer’s observation regarding eled expression. The eled+ cells in males that appear to be associated with vitellaria cells at 22 dpi (revised Supplementary Fig. 6b) may reflect either mis-assignment of germline cells by the UMAP algorithm (PMID: 35253834, the Fig1 in this reference illustrates this possibility) or the presence of a previously uncharacterized vitellaria-like population in males. We favor the latter explanation, as we observed some S1 Vitelline-like cells in males at 22 dpi (updated Supplementary Fig. 7c), suggesting that these cells may represent a male-specific vitellaria-like population rather than misclassified germline cells. This interpretation aligns with the work of George Wendt et al., who identified p48- and ataxin2-labeled vitellaria cells in males (PMID: 32973030), thereby confirming the long-standing observation that male parasites harbor low frequencies of vitellaria-like cells (PMID: 7200108).
11. In Figure 3E, lsamp and ddc expression seems to be partial in the delta-3 neuron cluster. Is this a gene coverage artifact from the scRNAseq or a reflection of the heterogeneity of delta-3 neurons? Quantifying their double FISH studies should be able to clarify this question.
Thank you for this insightful suggestion. Our scRNA-seq data indicate that nrps is expressed in approximately 89.5% of N4.3 neurons, while ddc and lsamp are detected in about 65.5% and 54.2% of these cells, respectively, suggesting potential heterogeneity (updated Supplementary Data 16). However, careful quantification with double-FISH reveals that both lsamp and ddc signals are present in nearly 100% of nrps+ neurons (Supplementary Fig. 20). We therefore propose that the seemingly heterogeneous pattern in the UMAP projection is more likely attributable to the limited sequencing depth of scRNA-seq, which can fail to detect low-abundance transcripts, rather than to true biological heterogeneity within the N4.3 neuronal population.
12. Unpaired two-tailed parametric t-tests were widely used for the statistics. Have all the data passed a normality test?
We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this critical point concerning data normality and the use of parametric testing. We have reassessed the normality of all relevant datasets using the D'Agostino & Pearson test (Supplementary Data 27). The majority of the data, including those in Fig. 4d–h and the updated Supplementary Fig. 22, were found to be normally distributed. However, the D8 and D20 datasets in the updated Supplementary Fig. 22a and b, as well as the worm BATT data in Fig. 4i, deviated from normality. For these non-normally distributed datasets, we reapplied the non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test (two-tailed) for group comparisons (Supplementary Data 28). The results are fully consistent with the original conclusions. And we have updated the Methods section to include a detailed description of this statistical approach (lines 794-802).
13. Besides the top three genes, nrps, lsamp, and ddc, what other genes and associated pathways are specific to delta-3 neurons? Can the authors elaborate on this further?
We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. In addition to nrps, lsamp, and ddc, we now provide a list of driver genes (Supplementary Data 19) and associated pathways (Supplementary Data 20) are specific to the N4.3 neuron (formerly delta-3).
14. For IF images, please add quantification and experimental replications in the figure legends.
Thanks, added.
15. Line 347: “worms treated with lsamp dsRNA instead of ddc dsRNA lost their ability…” This statement would be more effective omitting mention of ddc dsRNA here. First, state what happens after lsamp dsRNA treatment, then say that ddc dsRNA treatment did not affect female sexual development.
Thank you. We have revised the text as suggested to make the statement more concise and effective in lines 341-348: “By employing RNAi in vitro, we found the male worms treated with lsamp dsRNA lost their ability to initiate female sexual development (Fig. 4a-b). These female worms paired with lsamp RNAi males displayed reduced Fast Blue BB staining in their vitellaria and possessed poorly developed ovaries (Fig. 4b). In addition, they barely laid eggs (Fig. 4c). The qRT-PCR result indicated a strong reduction of the lsamp expression in the male worms after the lsamp RNAi (Fig. 4d). In contrast, treatment with ddc dsRNA did not affect female sexual development (Supplementary Fig. 21). The above results suggest that male lsamp is essential for female sexual development.”
16. Line 398: “Acetylated alpha-tubulin is a protein that stabilizes microtubules” is an awkward statement. Acetylation of alpha-tubulin (a subunit of the microtubule polymer) is a post-translational modification of microtubules (on alpha-tubulin) associated with stable microtubules.
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We have revised the sentence to more accurately describe the relationship between α-tubulin acetylation and microtubule stability: “Acetylation of α-tubulin, a post-translational modification of microtubules, is associated with microtubule stabilization and regulates cell morphology in nerve fibers.” (lines 394-395).
17. Line 469: “We… characterize gene regulatory programs…” This work did not characterize gene regulatory programs; it identified changes in gene expression associated with dimorphic sexual development.
Thanks. We have revised the wording to more accurately reflect our findings: "In the present study, we used single-cell RNA sequencing to systematically profile gene expression dynamics underlying dimorphic gametogenesis in S. japonicum." (lines 469-471).
18. Line 507: “…no active neurogenesis at the adult stage.” Single-cell sequencing does not suffice to make this claim. The population of neural progenitors may just be smaller than can be detected, given the number of cells sequenced here.
Thanks. We agree and have removed the corresponding statement.
19. “Gender” is a social construct, so the authors should omit that word and refer simply to the parasite’s sex.
Thank you. The term “gender” has been replaced throughout the manuscript with “sex”.
Reviewer #4:
1. I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
We sincerely appreciate your valuable contribution in reviewing our manuscript.
We sincerely appreciate the reviewers’ positive evaluation and recognition of our work. We would like to thank the reviewers for their thoughtful and helpful critiques of our work. The work is greatly improved upon the incorporation of their suggestions.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author)
The authors have made extensive changes to the manuscript and have addressed all our previous points comprehensively. The new version of the manuscript has been greatly improved, including a streamlined analysis of vitelline cell developmental trajectories, neural lineages, and germline gene expression dynamics. We remain enthusiastic about its publication and just have some minor suggestions to consider:
We appreciate your affirmation that our revisions have comprehensively addressed the previous points and greatly improved the manuscript. We have implemented the minor suggestions as detailed below.
1. Proportions of cell types
Analyses describing the proportions of cell types are still really prominent in the manuscript but we still don’t really feel that they add any new insights. The context for this comment is that the paper is huge with many figures, so we feel that making some reductions would further improve readability. The authors have swapped some figures between supplementary material and main text but we’re unclear how this improves the manuscript. figure 1c does confirm a couple of known things; for instance, it clearly shows that when vitellocyte cells are combined across the datasets, most come from mature females, as expected.
The figure (1c) legend text “…showing the relative proportions of key cell types in S. japonicum at different developmental stages” is a bit misleading. Each bar represents all cells of a given type from across multiple stages. It’s not the proportion of that type within the parasite. A better description might therefore be “…showing the relative proportions of cells from different stages within the cell types of the combined S. japonicum dataset”.
The composition analysis also doesn’t consistently support the narrative. For instance, it is true that “male … differentiated neural cells (e.g., non-ciliated neurons and ciliated neurons) continuously expanded” but the authors don’t mention that in females this is not the case.
Thank you for this constructive feedback regarding the prominence of cell-type proportion analyses and the overall readability of our manuscript. We have removed the Supplementary Fig 6a, and moved Fig 1c to the revised Supplementary Fig 6a. Correspondingly, we have shortened the related descriptions in the main text to reduce redundancy (lines 138-153).
We have also revised the figure legend of the revised Supplementary Fig 6a as suggested: “…showing the relative proportions of cells from different stages within the cell types of the combined S. japonicum dataset.” (in the updated Supplementary figure informations file)
Additionally, we have supplemented the description regarding the changes in neural cells in female worms: “In female worms, these populations did not show sustained expansion but rather exhibited an initial increase followed by a subsequent decline after 22 dpi, which is consistent with the weakening of neural activity in females after 22 dpi, as revealed by bulk RNA-seq analysis10 (Supplementary Fig. 6a-b, and Data 5).” (lines 150-153)
2. Convergent RNA trajectories
In discussing the convergent RNA velocity trajectories, the authors now hypothesise that the convergence point is “a shared multipotent progenitor pool that functions as a developmental hub capable of giving rise to multiple downstream cell types in both males and females.” They conclude that “This finding offers new insight into the hierarchical organization of gonadal cells in this organism, suggesting the presence of a common —rather than sex-specific —early developmental regulatory mechanism.” This seems like a lot to infer from RNA velocity alone, without additional validation. Some reference to published precedents from other systems is needed
Thank you for this insightful comment. We agree that inferring shared progenitors from RNA velocity alone requires caution. Our hypothesis was proposed to explain the convergent pattern observed in both sexes, and it is strongly supported by precedent: in S. mansoni, Wang et al. identified δ-neoblasts—somatic stem cells defined by high nanos-2, fgfrA, and fgfrB expression—as multipotent progenitors for both sexes (PMID: 29988015). The convergent SSCs-2 cluster in our data shows a highly similar molecular signature. Therefore, our RNA velocity results likely reflect a conserved, shared multipotent progenitor pool analogous to δ-neoblasts, extending this model to S. japonicum.
We have cited the relevant paper (PMID: 29988015) and revised the Discussion section in lines 476-483: “Although our RNA velocity analysis of sex-related subsets revealed clear trajectories from GSCs to their progeny, it consistently showed convergence toward a central cell state identified as SSCs-2 in both sexes (Fig. 2b). SSCs-2 population shares high expression of key markers (e.g., nanos-2, fgfrA, fgfrB) with the multipotent δ-neoblasts, which constitute a shared somatic stem cell pool in S. mansoni18. We therefore hypothesize that this convergence point may represent a similar, shared multipotent progenitor pool, capable of giving rise to multiple downstream cell types in both males and females, which requires further experimental validation.”
3. The last sentence of the results (“These results provide new insights into male-female interactions during sexual development in schistosomes and may inform future strategies for combating schistosomiasis ” ) is more of a discussion/conclusion statement. It’s also very similar to that last sentence of the Discussion, so I suggest removing it from Results.
Thank you. We have deleted this sentence.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
We sincerely appreciate your valuable contribution in reviewing our manuscript.

The authors have satisfactorily addressed the concerns of the referees and the revised manuscript is ready for publication.
We sincerely appreciate your recognition of our work.
